Multiple proteins now point toward the same vascular effects: the activin ligands INHBA and INHBB, plus ENG, ACVRL1, and GDF2 from the BMP9–ALK1–endoglin pathway behind hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. That convergence gives strong support for telangiectasia, epistaxis, and bleeding as the leading adverse-event signals.

I'm also starting to look at ACVR1 (ALK2), which ranks 14th with a score of 0.37.

I'm working through ACVR1 next: its gain-of-function mutations cause FOP, and since it mainly signals through BMPs, inhibiting it could affect bone development, though that evidence is speculative. I'll keep that as an uncertain possibility. I'm also turning to the activin type I receptors ACVR1B and ACVR1C, which play roles in the reproductive and neuroendocrine axis.

I'm looking at ACVR1B and ACVR2A/ACVR2B as the shared activin receptors on pituitary gonadotropes. INHBB forms inhibin B with the alpha subunit, which suppresses FSH, while activin B promotes it. If the intervention neutralizes activin B and activin A, that removes the FSH stimulation, which would fit the impaired fertility already expected from the sotatercept label.

Now I'm turning to the BMP ligands (BMP2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8A, 8B, 10) and their receptors BMPR1A, BMPR1B, and BMPR2. They rank lower and are structurally related superfamily members, so I'm treating them as uncertain, since an activin-directed agent wouldn't obviously cross-react with them and I have no evidence of toxicity from them specifically.

I'm weighing BMP10 next: its rank is low at 42 with a score of 0.08, but it signals through the same ALK1-endoglin pathway in endothelium as BMP9, so it could add to the telangiectasia and bleeding picture as a contributing factor.

I'm now looking at PTGER3, the prostaglandin EP3 receptor, which ranks second with a very high score of 0.84. It has no clear biological link to the INHBB or activin pathway, so this may be an algorithmic artifact or an unknown off-target, and I'll treat it as uncertain.

I'm weighing PTGER3, the prostaglandin EP3 receptor, which scores very high at 0.84 yet has no mechanistic link to activin or TGF-beta signaling. EP3 is a GPCR and structurally unrelated to these cystine-knot ligands, so I'll treat it as uncertain: either a real unexpected off-target or an algorithmic artifact.

I'm now weighing PTGER3 as an exclusion: the prostaglandin EP3 receptor has no structural or pathway link to activin or TGF-beta signaling, and I can't tell which direction an off-target effect would push, so despite its high score I'll leave its adverse events out.

I'm running through the remaining GPCRs and unrelated membrane proteins, which have low scores and no mechanistic link to activin or BMP signaling, so I'm treating them as likely artifacts. I'm also checking PMEPA1, which I know as an intracellular negative regulator of TGF-beta signaling, though it doesn't clearly connect to a ligand-directed agent.

I'm going through the remaining proteins: several membrane and signaling molecules like GINM1, CD79B, and DLK1, which have low scores and no clear shared pathway with the activin or BMP ligands, so I'm treating them as likely non-specific hits. I'm now settling the adverse-event list: the intracellular PMEPA1 and LDLRAD4 stay out since they're not reachable by an extracellular agent. Telangiectasia comes first, supported by INHBA and INHBB through activin inhibition and by ENG via the HHT pathway.

Next I'm checking the epistaxis signal, which lines up with the same convergence around ENG, ACVRL1, and GDF2, plus the activin inhibition from INHBA and INHBB, and the sotatercept figures back it up. I'm adding GI bleeding as a fifth adverse-event term, since it follows from the thrombocytopenia and telangiectasia convergence on INHBA, INHBB, ENG, and ACVRL1, and the label reports it at 11.6% versus none on placebo.

I'm moving on to the serious adverse events: embryo-fetal toxicity, since activin signaling through INHBA and INHBB matters for embryonic development, and impaired fertility, since activin stimulates FSH through the HPG axis. I'm also starting on the postmarketing cerebral hemorrhage signal, which is tied to the vascular effects.

I'm weighing ascites as the last adverse-event candidate: it's only a postmarketing signal, and the source itself offers just a speculative mechanism through right heart dysfunction, so I'm leaning toward leaving it out.

I'm dropping ascites because its proposed mechanism only fits the PAH population and doesn't follow from the protein perturbation itself. I'm weighing TGFBR1 and TGFBR2 kinase-inhibitor evidence, which is about cardiac valve and cartilage effects, but this intervention seems to act extracellularly by binding ligands or receptors rather than inhibiting kinases. The cartilage and growth plate effects I'd be counting on come from kinase inhibitors and animal toxicology studies, though, so I'm treating this as low-to-medium confidence.

I'm dropping the GDF2 and BMP9 idea for now, since dalantercept has no human adverse-event data behind it and only fits the ENG/ACVRL1 convergence as a mechanistic story. Still, human genetics fills the gap: HHT1 and HHT2 are caused by loss-of-function mutations in ENG and ACVRL1, which is well-established support for the telangiectasia link.

I'm treating HHT as a human genetic anchor: loss-of-function variants in ENG and ACVRL1 are the classic cause of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, which already explains the telangiectasia and bleeding pattern without needing retrieved notes for those genes. I'm now assessing the type II activin receptors, ACVR2A and ACVR2B, which pair with ALK4 and ALK7 to carry activin A and B signaling. If the intervention neutralizes INHBA and INHBB, those downstream receptor interactions would be blocked as well.

The sotatercept label already lists platelet decrease as a direct adverse reaction, so I'll use that as the anchor for this one.

entries.response_reasoning:
**STEP 1: TRIAGE AND PER-PROTEIN ANALYSIS**

Assumption about intervention: Given that INHBB (P09529, the protein this list was generated for) sits at rank 1 with a perfect normalized score (1.00), and the next-highest biologically coherent hits are INHBA (activin A, rank 3) and TGFBR2 (rank 4), the most parsimonious reading is that this is a secreted-ligand-directed biologic (e.g., a neutralizing antibody or receptor-ectodomain trap) targeting activin B (INHBB) with cross-reactivity to the closely homologous activin A (INHBA) subunit, consistent with the "activin trap" drug class (e.g., sotatercept/luspatercept-like ActRII-Fc molecules) for which detailed human safety data were retrieved. I assume the intervention is a large biologic that does **not** cross the plasma membrane and therefore can only engage extracellular/cell-surface/secreted proteins.

**Intended target (exempted from triage):**
- **INHBB (P09529)** – Secreted. Forms activin B (homodimer) or inhibin B (with alpha subunit). Signals through ACVR2A/ACVR2B + ACVR1B/ACVR1C (ALK4/ALK7) → SMAD2/3. Physiologically regulates FSH secretion (pituitary), erythropoiesis, vascular homeostasis, reproductive tissue function, wound healing/fibrosis. Rank 1/score 1.00 – treated as the designed target, direction of perturbation = neutralization/antagonism of activin B signaling.

**Likely perturbed (biologically coherent extension of the same ligand/pathway):**
- **INHBA (P08476)** – Secreted activin A subunit, near-identical receptor usage to INHBB (ACVR2A/2B, ACVR1B). High homology to INHBB makes cross-neutralization plausible; rank 3/score 0.69 is consistent with this. Direct human pharmacological evidence exists for agents trapping/inhibiting INHBA (sotatercept, garetosmab) — extensive labeled and postmarketing safety data. Direction: antagonism of activin A signaling.
- **ACVR2A (P27037), ACVR2B (Q13705), ACVR1B (P36896), ACVR1C (Q8NER5)** – Type I/II activin receptors; cell-membrane, accessible. These are the obligate receptor partners for INHBA/INHBB signaling. If the ligands are neutralized, downstream receptor engagement falls correspondingly (pathway_effect rather than direct_target_effect). Scores are modest (0.11–0.47); independent pharmacology exists for ACVR2B (bimagrumab) and ACVR2A (cited in sotatercept postmarketing study), supporting pathway-level relevance.
- **ENG (P17813, Endoglin)** and **ACVRL1 (P37023, ALK1)** – Cell-membrane endothelial co-receptor/receptor for BMP9/10. Human genetics: loss-of-function mutations in ENG (HHT1) and ACVRL1 (HHT2) cause hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (mucocutaneous telangiectasia, epistaxis, GI bleeding, AVMs) — well-established human genetic evidence. If the intervention perturbs this endothelial stabilization axis (directly, or indirectly by shifting the activin/BMP signaling balance across shared SMAD machinery), it converges mechanistically with the activin-trap vascular phenotype already seen clinically with sotatercept (telangiectasia, epistaxis). Scores 0.45 (ENG) and 0.15 (ACVRL1) are moderate; treated as "likely perturbed" based on coherent biology plus human genetic precedent, not on score alone.
- **GDF2 (Q9UK05, BMP9)** – Secreted ligand for ACVRL1/ENG; rank 8/score 0.47. Same vascular-integrity axis as above. A ligand trap (dalantercept, ChEMBL) exists but no human safety signal is retrieved; included as a mechanistic contributor to the ENG/ACVRL1 vascular cluster, not as an independent AE source.
- **BMP10 (O95393)** – Second ligand for ACVRL1/ENG, rank 42/score 0.08 (low score, but biologically same axis). Treated as a minor contributing/convergent protein only.

**Uncertain (plausible but weakly supported):**
- **TGFBR2 (P37173)** – Rank 4/score 0.68; cell-membrane, accessible, canonical TGF-β type II receptor. No independent pharmacological evidence links a ligand-trap/antibody of this kind to TGFBR2 engagement; the only retrieved evidence concerns small-molecule ALK5 (TGFBR1) kinase inhibitors, a different modality and mechanism. Treated as uncertain; evidence for cardiac valvulopathy/physeal dysplasia is animal/nonclinical only, so per rules it cannot support a prediction on its own and is dropped.
- **TGFBR1 (P36897)** – Rank 25/score 0.25; same reasoning as TGFBR2. Animal-only evidence; dropped.
- **BMPR2 (Q13873), BMPR1A (P36894), BMPR1B (O00238), AMHR2 (Q16671)** – Cell-membrane TGF-β superfamily receptors; plausible structural cross-reactivity given family membership, but no pharmacological precedent or independent evidence retrieved. Scores low–moderate (0.01–0.26). Uncertain; no AE generated.
- **ACVR1 (Q04771)** – Membrane, rank 14/score 0.37. Associated with FOP (gain-of-function) in humans, but no evidence an extracellular ligand trap of INHBB/INHBA would meaningfully antagonize ACVR1 signaling (ACVR1 is mainly a BMP type I receptor, not a principal activin A/B receptor in most tissues). Uncertain; no independent evidence; no AE generated.
- **BMP2, BMP4, BMP5, BMP6, BMP7, BMP8A, BMP8B, NODAL, INHBC, INHBE** – All secreted TGF-β superfamily ligands, accessible in principle, but no retrieved pharmacological or genetic evidence connects toxicity of an activin-B-directed intervention to these distant family members. Scores are low-to-moderate (0.12–0.38) but score is only a weak signal per instructions. Treated as uncertain; no independent evidence to support a specific AE; not carried forward.
- **PTGER3 (P43115)** – Rank 2/score 0.84 (very high), cell-membrane GPCR. No structural, pathway, or pharmacological relationship to the TGF-β/activin ligand-trap mechanism exists; EP3 is a 7TM GPCR, mechanistically unrelated to a cystine-knot secreted ligand or its receptors. This pattern (very high score, no plausible biological link) is most consistent with a prediction artifact. Direction of any true perturbation (agonism vs antagonism) is also unknown. Rated uncertain/likely artifact; retrieved misoprostol/dinoprostone boxed warnings describe EP3 **agonist** drug toxicity (teratogenicity from uterotonic activity), which does not establish that this intervention — an unrelated modality with unknown action at EP3 — would produce the same effect. No AE generated.
- **PTGFR, PTGER1, TBXA2R, GRPR, NMBR** – Unrelated GPCRs, low scores (0.05–0.16), no pathway/structural link to the TGF-β superfamily, no supporting evidence. Unlikely perturbed/artifact; no AE.

**Unlikely perturbed (accessibility or non-specificity objections):**
- **PMEPA1/TMEPAI (Q969W9)** – Early endosome/Golgi membrane, intracellular-facing; inaccessible to an extracellular biologic. Unlikely perturbed.
- **LDLRAD4 (O15165)** – Early endosome membrane; intracellular. Unlikely perturbed.
- **PEG10 (Q86TG7)** – Cytoplasm/nucleus (extracellular vesicle membrane component is a minor fraction); largely intracellular. Unlikely perturbed.
- **SCRIB, RNF11, SYNJ2BP, HEPACAM2** – Cytoplasmic/nuclear/organelle-membrane proteins; inaccessible. Unlikely perturbed.
- **CDC50A, CDC50B** – Membrane flippase chaperones; no pharmacological precedent linking them to this ligand class; low biological rationale despite membrane location. Unlikely perturbed/artifact.
- **HAVCR2, CD79B, IZUMO1, GINM1, MRAP2, LRRIQ1, PRSS50, DLK1** – No shared pathway, no pharmacological precedent, scores low-moderate but with no independent support; classic pattern of incidental high-rank noise in a 50-protein output. Unlikely to be functionally perturbed; no AE generated.

**STEP 2–4: KEY PROTEIN–AE RELATIONSHIPS (convergent mechanisms)**

*Vascular/haemorrhagic cluster (INHBA, INHBB, ENG, ACVRL1, GDF2, BMP10):*
Activin A/B signaling through ACVR2A/2B-ACVR1B (SMAD2/3) and the parallel BMP9/10-ACVRL1-ENG (SMAD1/5/8) endothelial-stabilization axis both regulate vascular integrity. Neutralization of INHBA/INHBB (direct human pharmacological evidence from sotatercept) plus any coincidental engagement of the ENG/ACVRL1/GDF2/BMP10 axis (supported by human HHT genetics) converge on a common phenotype: mucocutaneous telangiectasia, epistaxis, and mucosal bleeding (GI, gingival). This is a convergent_multi_protein_effect.

*Erythropoiesis (INHBA, INHBB → ACVR2A/2B):*
Activin A/B normally restrains late-stage erythroid maturation via SMAD2/3; neutralizing these ligands removes this brake, increasing haemoglobin/red cell mass (erythrocytosis), directly evidenced in the sotatercept label.

*Platelet production (INHBA, INHBB):*
Activin/SMAD2/3 signaling influences megakaryocyte maturation; neutralization is associated with severe thrombocytopenia in the same drug class (label warning), though the precise cellular mechanism is less granular.

*Reproductive/HPG axis (INHBA, INHBB, ACVR1B, ACVR2A, ACVR2B):*
Activins stimulate pituitary FSH synthesis/secretion and are essential for gonadal and placental development; neutralization is mechanistically expected to impair fertility and pose embryo-fetal risk, consistent with the labeled warnings for the same ligand-trap class.

*Vascular/haemodynamic (INHBA, INHBB, with ENG/ACVRL1 as amplifiers):*
Altered vascular remodeling balance (activin vs BMP arms) is associated with hypertension and, via combined thrombocytopenia + vascular fragility, with rare but serious cerebral haemorrhage (postmarketing pharmacovigilance signal for the same drug class).

**STEP 6: Overall severity distribution**
Weighted by frequency, the bulk of expected cases are mild/moderate mucocutaneous and constitutional events (epistaxis, telangiectasia, rash, headache, dizziness, diarrhoea, erythema, erythrocytosis), with a smaller but clinically important share of severe events (thrombocytopenia, GI haemorrhage, hypertension, cerebral haemorrhage) and a small fatal/severe-category fraction (embryo-fetal toxicity, rare fatal haemorrhage).

Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
chunks.text: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Sotatercept, a first-in-class activin signalling inhibitor, represents a novel therapeutic advancement for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a progressive and life-threatening condition characterised by pulmonary vascular remodelling and right ventricular dysfunction. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS The first large-scale Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System analysis, 48 safety signals (18 unlabelled) and the critical discovery of cerebral haemorrhage and ascites as important medical events. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Emphasises the clinical implications for monitoring protocols and regulatory pharmacovigilance. Introduction Sotatercept, a first-in-class activin signalling inhibitor, represents a novel therapeutic advancement for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a progressive and life-threatening condition characterised by pulmonary vascular remodelling and right ventricular dysfunction. By targeting the imbalance between proproliferative activin signalling and antiproliferative bone morphogenetic protein pathways, sotatercept addresses the underlying pathophysiology of PAH, offering potential disease-modifying effects. Clinical trials, including the pivotal PULSAR and STELLAR studies, have demonstrated its efficacy in reducing pulmonary vascular resistance, improving exercise capacity and delaying clinical worsening. These findings supported its Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval on 26 March 2024 for adults with PAH, establishing it as a critical addition to existing therapies. Despite its therapeutic benefits, emerging safety data from clinical trials highlight specific risks, including thrombocytopenia, haemoglobin elevation and telangiectasia. Notably, the ZENITH trial identified life-threatening adverse events (AEs)—including cardiac arrest—in patients with advanced PAH, highlighting potential risks in vulnerable populations. Following sotatercept’s FDA approval and the limitations of premarketing studies, including small sample sizes and controlled environments, postmarketing pharmacovigilance is vital to evaluate its safety in diverse real-world populations. This pharmacovigilance study uses real-world data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) to systematically evaluate the safety profile of sotatercept. We identified key safety signals by quantifying AE frequency and disproportionality, investigated unlisted preferred terms (PTs) to detect potential risks and classified AEs by severity using the EudraVigilance Expert Working Group’s IME (Important Medical Events) list (V.28.0). By integrating these analyses, this study aims to bridge knowledge gaps between clinical trial evidence and real-world safety outcomes, ensuring safer utilisation of this groundbreaking

chunks.title: Nonclinical Profile of PF-06952229 (MDV6058), a Novel TGFβRI/Activin Like Kinase 5 Inhibitor Supports Clinical Evaluation in Cancer.
chunks.journal: The Journal of pharmacology and experimental therapeutics
mesh_terms: Receptor, Transforming Growth Factor-beta Type I
chunks.text: The development of transforming growth factor βreceptor inhibitors (TGFβRi) as new medicines has been affected by cardiac valvulopathy and arteriopathy toxicity findings in nonclinical toxicology studies. PF-06952229 (MDV6058) selected using rational drug design is a potent and selective TGFβRI inhibitor with a relatively clean off-target selectivity profile and good pharmacokinetic properties across species. PF-06952229 inhibited clinically translatable phospho-SMAD2 biomarker (≥60%) in human and cynomolgus monkey peripheral blood mononuclear cells, as well as in mouse and rat splenocytes. Using an optimized, intermittent dosing schedule (7-day on/7-day off/cycle; 5 cycles), PF-06952229 demonstrated efficacy in a 63-day syngeneic MC38 colon carcinoma mouse model. In the pivotal repeat-dose toxicity studies (rat and cynomolgus monkey), PF-06952229 on an intermittent dosing schedule (5-day on/5-day off cycle; 5 cycles, 28 doses) showed no cardiac-related adverse findings. However, new toxicity findings related to PF-06952229 included reversible hepatocellular (hepatocyte necrosis with corresponding clinically monitorable transaminase increases) and lung (hemorrhage with mixed cell inflammation) findings at ≥ targeted projected clinical efficacious exposures. Furthermore, partially reversible cartilage hypertrophy (trachea and femur in rat; femur in monkey) and partially to fully reversible, clinically monitorable decreases in serum phosphorus and urinary phosphate at ≥ projected clinically efficacious exposures were observed. Given the integral role of TGFβ in endochondral bone formation, cartilage findings in toxicity studies have been observed with other TGFβRi classes of compounds. The favorable cumulative profile of PF-06952229 in biochemical, pharmacodynamic, pharmacokinetic, and nonclinical studies allowed for its evaluation in cancer patients using the intermittent dosing schedule (7-day on/7-day off) and careful protocol-defined monitoring. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Only a few TGFβRi have progressed for clinical evaluation due to adverse cardiac findings in pivotal nonclinical toxicity studies. The potential translations of such findings in patients are of major concern. Using a carefully optimized intermittent dosing schedule, PF-06952229 has demonstrated impressive pharmacological efficacy in the syngeneic MC38 colon carcinoma mouse model. Additionally, a nonclinical toxicology package without cardiovascular liabilities and generally monitorable toxicity profile has been completed. The compound presents an acceptable International Conference on Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Registration of Pharmaceuticals for Human Use S9-compliant profile for the intended-to-treat cancer patients.

chunks.title: Drug-induced Physeal Abnormalities in Preclinical Toxicity Studies.
mesh_terms: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
chunks.text: Most toxic physeal changes are characterized microscopically by altered chondrocyte development, proliferation, or maturation in the growth plate and eventually result in disordered appositional bone growth. Many therapeutic drugs directly or indirectly target proteins involved in chondrocytic differentiation and maturation pathways, so toxic physeal injury has become increasingly common in preclinical toxicologic pathology. While physeal dysplasia has been associated with several different drug classes including bisphosphonates, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor inhibitors, fibroblast growth factor receptor inhibitors, transforming growth factor beta receptor inhibitors, and vascular targeting agents, physeal changes often share similar morphologic features including thickening and disorganization of the hypertrophic layer, increased numbers of hypertrophic chondrocytes, altered mineralization of endochondral ossification, and/or increased thickness of subphyseal bone. Knowledge of genetic and nutritional diseases affecting bone growth has been important in helping to determine which specific target drugs may be affecting that could result in toxic physeal lesions. A pathophysiologic mechanism for most physeal toxicants has been determined in detail using a variety of investigative techniques. However, due to the signaling cross talk and the tight regulation required for chondrocyte maturation in the physis, several growth factor pathways are likely to be affected simultaneously with pharmacologic disruption of physeal homeostasis and inhibition of one factor necessary for chondrocyte function often affects others.

chunks.title: Postmarketing analysis of sotatercept: identifying serious unlabelled events.
mesh_terms: United States Food and Drug Administration
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
chunks.text: Cerebral haemorrhage may be linked to sotatercept’s haematological effects, including thrombocytopenia, which could exacerbate bleeding risk, particularly in patients receiving concomitant anticoagulants or antiplatelet therapies. Additionally, sotatercept-associated hypertension (3.4% vs 1.6% in the pooled PULSAR/STELLAR analysis) might contribute to cerebral vascular stress, while its mechanism as an activin signalling inhibitor may theoretically influence vascular remodelling and microvascular integrity, as suggested by telangiectasia development. However, establishing definitive causality is challenging given the multifactorial nature of cerebral haemorrhage in patients with PAH, where disease progression, concurrent medications (particularly anticoagulants), comorbidities and baseline bleeding risks may all contribute to these events. Nevertheless, identifying these potential safety signals through early postmarketing surveillance provides valuable clinical warnings that warrant further investigation. Controlled studies with adequate confounder adjustment are needed to clarify the true relationship between sotatercept and cerebral haemorrhage. Ascites may reflect the progression of right heart dysfunction in advanced PAH. Although sotatercept improves pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular remodelling, transient haemodynamic shifts or the unmasking of latent left ventricular dysfunction (due to reduced right heart afterload) could paradoxically exacerbate systemic congestion in vulnerable individuals. In addition, patients with PAH and comorbid portal hypertension (eg, from heritable or connective tissue disease-associated subtypes) may be more susceptible to ascites due to splanchnic venous congestion, though this remains speculative. Clarification of whether these events are linked to disease progression or sotatercept’s pharmacodynamics is needed, but current data are insufficient for definitive conclusions. Prospective studies are required to clarify these relationships. Until then, clinicians should remain vigilant for ascites in sotatercept-treated patients. Gender-specific and reporter-specific analyses reveal distinct patterns in the safety profile of sotatercept. Women contributed a greater number of AE reports, which aligns with the higher prevalence of PAH in the female population. However, the disproportionality signal for haematological abnormalities was stronger among men, suggesting that haemoglobin and haematocrit elevations, though less frequent, tend to be more pronounced in male patients. The underlying cause remains uncertain, but it may reflect sex-related differences in drug-induced erythropoiesis or baseline haematological parameters that accentuate these changes in men, warranting further investigation to elucidate these mechanisms. chunks.title: The short-term effects of repetitive E. coli-derived rhBMP-2 administration through intravenous injection in rats.
chunks.text: Escherichia coli-derived recombinant human (rh)BMP-2 (E.BMP-2) can be used as a bone graft substitute because to its high osteoinductivity, but its toxicity is not well understood. Thus, we report on the toxicity of E.BMP-2 in Sprague-Dawley rats under the condition of repetitive injection for 2 weeks. Randomly selected 10 male and female rats were administered with E.BMP-2 at a dose of 0.05, 0.18 or 0.5 mg/kg as an experimental group. A control group with another 10 rats was given E.BMP-2 carrier. Both E.BMP-2 and E.BMP-2 carrier were administered through intravenous injection for 2 weeks. For toxicokinetics study, 3 male and female rats were randomly selected from each group. During the observation period, general symptom, weight and food intakes were monitored, and ophthalmic and urine tests were performed as well. After the observation period, all animals were subjected to blood test, biochemical analysis and organ-weight measurement. During autopsy, visual inspections and histopathological examinations were done. Toxicokinetics study confirmed systemic exposure of the test material. No death or abnormal clinical sign was found during the injection period. Toxicity changes induced by the injection were not detected in autopsy or the tests for weight, food intakes, ophthalmology, hematology and serum biochemistry. The female groups administered with 0.18 and 0.5 mg/kg (the female 0.18-mg/kg group and the female 0.5-mg/kg group) showed absolute and relative weight loss in ovaries and reduced corpora lutea. It was the expected pharmacologic activity, rather than toxicity. The histopathological test revealed cartilage formation and increased fibroblast around the tail vein, but these were thought to be the result of osteoinductivity of the test material. In the male group with 0.5 mg/kg of E.BMP-2 (the male 0.5-mg/kg group), local appearance of multinucleated cells in lung parenchyma was observed, but it was considered as the natural reaction to remove E.BMP-2, which is a recombinant protein. In toxicokinetics study, systemic exposure (area under the serum concentration-time curve and maximum observed serum concentration) increased as the injection dose was increased in both male and female rats, and no clear difference was noticed between the sexes. Blood drug content did not change during the injection period, but the half-life was shortened as the injection dose was increased. Under the condition of this study, the no observed adverse effects level of E.BMP-2 was over 0.5 mg/kg in both male and female rats.

I'm looking at the predicted interaction profile for the intervention, where INHBB ranks first with a score of 1.00, followed by PTGER3, INHBA, and TGFBR2, and then a long tail of mostly TGF-beta, activin, and BMP family proteins.

I'm weighing whether this ligand-trap reading holds, since the activin, BMP, and TGF-beta receptors all show up in the interaction profile. The ranking of PTGER3 second is the surprising part, because it belongs to a different family from the rest of the list.

I'm going through the rest of the interaction list: the BMP, activin, and TGF-beta receptors and ligands, plus a few unrelated proteins like PRSS50, CD79B, and the prostaglandin and thromboxane receptors. It all points toward an activin-pathway ligand trap, one that would sit in the same space as the soluble receptors on that list.

I'm now looking at whether PTGER3's rank of 0.84 is a real signal or an artifact, since prostaglandin receptors are GPCRs with no structural relation to the TGF-beta superfamily. The same goes for the other prostaglandin and thromboxane receptors and GRPR and NMBR, which bind small molecules, so I'm treating those hits as likely spurious for a protein-based intervention.

I'm now weighing the ligand-trap reading against the rest of the list, which points toward a soluble receptor fusion that would capture activin and BMP ligands. The prostaglandin and GRPR/NMBR hits are still unlikely to fit a protein-based agent, so I'm setting them aside as probable noise.

I'm moving through the candidate list and checking the activin, BMP, and TGF-beta receptors against the ligand-trap idea, and I'm starting to plan the expected adverse effects around that mechanism. Now I'm going through the list one protein at a time, beginning with INHBB, which is the intended target at rank 1 with a score of 1.00.

I'm now treating INHBB as the intended target, a secreted activin B subunit that forms activin B or inhibin B and signals through the activin receptors to regulate FSH and gonadal function. Given the intervention is aimed at it, I'm assuming it neutralizes or traps the activin B ligand, though that rests on the rank and score alone.

I'm checking PTGER3, ranked second at 0.84, against the rest of the list. It's a GPCR with no structural link to the TGF-beta superfamily, so it looks like an artifact, and I'd rate it unlikely for a protein-based intervention, though I can't rule it out without knowing what the intervention actually is.

I'm weighing PTGER3 at 0.84 against its biology: it's a membrane GPCR with no structural tie to the activin and TGF-beta network, so a protein ligand trap shouldn't plausibly bind it. Unless the intervention was built to hit it, I'm inclined to call this a likely artifact, though the high score keeps me from fully ruling it out.

I'm marking the GPCR hits as unlikely perturbed, since prostaglandin, thromboxane, GRPR, and NMBR receptors are small-molecule or peptide receptors with no structural overlap with TGF-beta superfamily ligands or an INHBB-based biologic. I'll treat them as probable computational noise and label them accordingly.

I'm marking the prostaglandin, thromboxane, GRPR, and NMBR receptors as probable noise, since they bind small molecules or peptides with no link to the activin network. Next is INHBA, which I'm checking for cross-reactivity with INHBB given their high sequence similarity and shared receptor usage, so it looks likely to be perturbed too.

I'm checking TGFBR2, ranked fourth at 0.68, which is a TGF-beta receptor that normally binds TGF-beta ligands rather than activins. Because it sits in the top four and the superfamily receptors share structural folds, I'm not ready to rule it out, though I have no specific precedent for an activin B trap reaching it.

I'm turning to LRRIQ1, which is rank 5 with a score of 0.57. It has no known function annotation and no subcellular location in the data, so I can't judge whether it's accessible to the intervention, and I'll mark it as uncertain.

I'm going through the last few proteins on the list: PEG10, which has a mix of extracellular vesicle, cytoplasmic, and nuclear localization with no pharmacological precedent, and LDLRAD4, which sits on the early endosome membrane and so is unlikely to be reached from outside the cell. I'm marking both as unlikely to be perturbed and not generating any adverse-effect mechanism for them.

I'm now considering GDF2 (BMP9), which signals through ALK1 and BMPR2 in endothelial cells and is already the target of an existing ActRIIB-Fc trap, dalantercept, so it's a plausible candidate for the same kind of ligand-trap effect.

I'm now working through the remaining candidates, starting with GDF2. The ActRII-related receptors and ENG and BMPR2 on the list suggest the intervention may engage the GDF2–ALK1 endothelial axis, so I'm marking GDF2 as likely perturbed. Next up is ACVR1.

I'm now looking at ACVR1B (ALK4), a type I receptor for activin and GDF8/11 that pairs with the ACVR2A/B co-receptors. Since INHBB is the ligand being targeted, any reduced signaling through this receptor would likely come from ligand sequestration rather than the intervention binding the receptor directly, so I'm marking it as likely perturbed in the functional sense.

I'm working through the remaining receptors on the list, from ACVR1B through AMHR2, and asking whether the intervention would reduce their signaling by sequestering the ligands they bind, rather than by binding the receptors themselves. I'm treating the direct ligand-binding proteins, INHBB, INHBA, INHBC, INHBE, and GDF2, as the ones the intervention would actually reach. I'm going through the last few candidates: GINM1 has no known function or precedent, so I'm treating it as noise, and PRSS50 is an intracellular testis protease that the intervention couldn't reach. I'm running through the last few membrane-bound and intracellular candidates. SCRIB is a predominantly intracellular scaffold, and CDC50B is a flippase subunit with no connection to the pathway, so I'm marking both unlikely perturbed. HAVCR2 is next.

I'm going through the BMP ligands next, BMP2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8A, 8B, and 10, all secreted and so accessible to a biologic. I'm settling on the main picture: the intervention looks like an activin-type ligand trap, aimed mainly at INHBB with cross-reactivity to INHBA through homology. The weaker signals across other TGF-beta superfamily ligands and receptors would fit the known promiscuity of traps like this, similar to what the sotatercept evidence describes. I'm now listing the adverse events I'd expect from this kind of activin-pathway inhibition, anchored to the sotatercept evidence: epistaxis, telangiectasia, severe thrombocytopenia, erythrocytosis, bleeding events, headache, dizziness, rash, diarrhea, and erythema. I'm weighing the remaining adverse-event candidates now: embryo-fetal toxicity and impaired fertility look mechanistically plausible given activin's role in reproduction, while ascites seems tied to the PAH context, so I'm holding it at low confidence.

I'm working through how activin signaling normally runs in endothelial cells, where activin and the BMP9/ALK1 pathway push in opposite directions, so blocking activin could tip the balance toward BMP/SMAD1/5/8 signaling and drive the vascular changes linked to telangiectasia.

I'm connecting the endothelial side of this: activin ligands, BMP9 (GDF2), endoglin, and ACVRL1 all feed the same vascular quiescence pathway, so disrupting that balance could account for telangiectasia and epistaxis. I'm connecting the platelet and erythroid side next: activin signaling through ACVR2A/B and SMAD2/3 seems to restrain red cell maturation, so trapping it could lift erythrocytosis while also dampening megakaryocyte output and driving thrombocytopenia. I'm connecting the erythroid side here: activin signaling through SMAD2/3 holds back late-stage red cell maturation, so trapping it should lift hemoglobin and erythrocytosis. I'm also considering reproductive effects, since activin shapes FSH regulation and embryonic signaling, which would point toward impaired fertility and embryo-fetal toxicity risk.

I'm moving on to the GI and mucosal side, where bleeding from low platelets and fragile vessels could show up as GI or gingival bleeding alongside the epistaxis. I'm also considering headache, dizziness, rash, and erythema as less direct effects, plausibly tied to changes in blood viscosity or a hypersensitivity reaction to the biologic.

I'm weighing hypertension and cerebral hemorrhage as lower-confidence postmarketing signals, since the mechanism would be speculative: less activin signaling might leave BMP-driven vascular tone unopposed.

entries.response_reasoning:
**STEP 1: PROTEIN TRIAGE**

*Intended/primary target:* INHBB (Inhibin beta B chain, activin B subunit) is rank 1, score 1.00 — treated as the intended target per instructions (exempt from triage, analysed regardless of rank/score). Secreted, extracellular, readily accessible to a biologic. Direction of perturbation is not explicitly stated in the protein context; given the overall pattern of the list (dense cluster of activin/BMP ligands and their receptors, plus independent retrieved evidence for activin-trap pharmacology on INHBA/ACVR1B/ACVR2A/ACVRL1/BMPR1A/ACVR2B/BMP8B/GDF2), the most parsimonious inference is that the intervention is a ligand-trap/neutralizing biologic reducing INHBB (activin B) signaling, with likely cross-reactivity to closely related ligands. **This direction is assumed, not given explicitly — this caps downstream confidence at medium throughout.**

*Likely perturbed (beyond the exempt target):*
- **INHBA (P08476)** — 69% homologous activin subunit to INHBB, forms activin A/AB; independent ChEMBL/FDA evidence shows agents of this class act on INHBA directly. Likely perturbed (cross-reactivity via shared receptor system and high sequence/structural similarity).

*Uncertain (plausible, lower independent evidence):*
- **GDF2/BMP9 (Q9UK05)** — secreted ligand for ACVRL1/ENG/BMPR2; known target of related ligand-traps (dalantercept). Uncertain-to-likely.
- **INHBC (P55103), INHBE (P58166), NODAL (Q96S42), BMP2/4/5/6/7/8A/8B/10** — secreted TGF-β superfamily ligands; plausible low-affinity cross-reactivity given family homology and known promiscuity of ActRII-type traps, but no protein-specific evidence. Uncertain.
- **ACVR1, ACVR1B, ACVR1C, ACVR2A, ACVR2B, ACVRL1, BMPR1A, BMPR1B, BMPR2, ENG, AMHR2** — type I/II receptors and co-receptors for the above ligands. Not necessarily bound directly, but their *signaling* is plausibly altered indirectly (ligand depletion) — functional pathway perturbation, uncertain-to-likely depending on ligand.
- **TGFBR1, TGFBR2** — structurally related receptor family but bind TGF-β1/2/3, not activins/BMPs typically; weaker precedent. Uncertain, lower weight.

*Unlikely perturbed (explicit reasons):*
- **PTGER3, PTGER1, PTGFR, TBXA2R, GRPR, NMBR** — all class-A GPCRs for small-molecule/peptide ligands structurally unrelated to the TGF-β superfamily network that dominates this list; no shared binding-site architecture with a growth-factor ligand/ligand-trap biologic; no pharmacological precedent for such cross-reactivity. Treated as non-specific computational noise despite PTGER3's high score (0.84) — score is not treated as evidence absent biological plausibility.
- **HAVCR2 (TIM-3)** — immune checkpoint receptor, cell-membrane accessible but no structural/functional link to activin biology. Likely artifact.
- **LDLRAD4** — early endosome membrane (intracellular face); despite a reported role modulating TGFBR1 turnover, this location is not reachable by an extracellular biologic. Accessibility objection noted despite functional tension.
- **PMEPA1, RNF11** — intracellular negative regulators of SMAD signaling; inaccessible to an extracellular agent.
- **PEG10, HEPACAM2, SYNJ2BP, SCRIB, PRSS50** — predominantly intracellular/organelle-membrane proteins; inaccessible.
- **CDC50A, CDC50B** — flippase subunits, no pathway connection, inaccessible to the relevant degree or non-specific.
- **MRAP2, IZUMO1, CD79B, GINM1, LRRIQ1** — membrane or unknown proteins with no functional/pharmacological connection to activin/BMP/TGF-β biology; treated as noise (or, for LRRIQ1, insufficient information to assess at all).

No adverse events are derived from the "unlikely perturbed" group.

**STEP 2: KEY PROTEIN–AE RELATIONSHIPS**

AE: Erythrocytosis / Haemoglobin increased
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA
Perturbation plausibility: INHBB likely perturbed (intended target); INHBA likely perturbed (homologous ligand, direct pharmacological precedent)
Relationship type: direct_target_effect; pathway_effect; convergent_multi_protein_effect
Direction of perturbation: Neutralization/antagonism of activin A/B signaling (assumed)
Mechanistic chain: Activin A/B → ACVR2A/B–ACVR1B → SMAD2/3 normally restrains terminal erythroid maturation in bone marrow → blockade removes this brake → expanded erythroid output → increased red cell mass/haemoglobin (days-to-weeks timescale)
Supporting evidence: Human pharmacological evidence (same pathway, FDA label “Increased hemoglobin” 13–15% vs 1.2% placebo)
Evidence strength: strong (pathway/mechanism), human pharmacological evidence class 3/4
Confidence of prediction: medium (capped by assumed direction)
Confidence rationale: mechanism is tight and evidence is human/quantitative, but antagonist-direction assumption caps confidence

AE: Epistaxis
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA, GDF2, ENG, ACVRL1
Perturbation plausibility: INHBB likely (target); INHBA likely; GDF2/ENG/ACVRL1 uncertain (plausible ligand-trap cross-reactivity / downstream pathway effect)
Relationship type: pathway_effect; convergent_multi_protein_effect; genetic_phenotype_support
Direction: reduced activin and reduced GDF2(BMP9)-ALK1-ENG-BMPR2 endothelial quiescence signaling
Mechanistic chain: Reduced BMP9/ALK1/ENG signaling destabilizes endothelial quiescence/vascular integrity (phenocopying the mechanism underlying hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia caused by ENG/ACVRL1 loss-of-function) → mucosal capillary fragility → nasal mucosal bleeding
Supporting evidence: Human pharmacological evidence (label, 36%) + human genetic evidence (ENG/ACVRL1 LOF → HHT epistaxis phenotype)
Evidence strength: strong
Confidence: medium (direction-assumption cap; genetic evidence independent of direction assumption raises strength but ceiling remains medium)
Confidence rationale: convergent genetic + pharmacological evidence is strong, but assumed antagonist direction still caps the tier

AE: Telangiectasia
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA, GDF2, ENG, ACVRL1
Perturbation plausibility: as above
Relationship type: pathway_effect; convergent_multi_protein_effect; genetic_phenotype_support
Mechanistic chain: same BMP9-ALK1-ENG-BMPR2 destabilization → focal dilated dermal/mucosal microvessels
Supporting evidence: label (27%), HHT genetics
Evidence strength: strong
Confidence: medium
Confidence rationale: same as epistaxis

AE: Severe thrombocytopenia
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA
Relationship type: pathway_effect
Mechanistic chain: Activin signaling via ACVR2A/B-ACVR1B influences megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor lineage allocation; blockade shifts differentiation toward erythroid lineage at relative expense of megakaryopoiesis, lowering platelet counts
Supporting evidence: Human pharmacological (labeled Warning 5.3) — frequency not quantified in retrieved text
Evidence strength: moderate
Confidence: medium (capped further by unquantified frequency, but still medium ceiling)
Confidence rationale: mechanism inferred, frequency estimated, direction assumed

AE: Gastrointestinal bleeding; Gingival bleeding
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA (thrombocytopenia) + ENG/ACVRL1/GDF2 (vascular fragility)
Relationship type: convergent_multi_protein_effect
Mechanistic chain: thrombocytopenia + mucosal vascular fragility jointly lower bleeding threshold at GI/oral mucosa
Supporting evidence: label (10%, 9%)
Evidence strength: strong (quantitative, same pathway)
Confidence: medium

AE: Headache, Dizziness, Rash, Diarrhea, Erythema
Protein(s): INHBA (direct), INHBB (homologous)
Relationship type: pharmacological_support; pathway_effect
Mechanistic chain: non-specific systemic/vascular/cutaneous effects of activin pathway blockade and biologic exposure (hemoglobin/viscosity shifts, cutaneous microvascular change, generic biologic-related symptoms); exact single-step mechanism not fully elucidated
Supporting evidence: human pharmacological, same protein, quantitative (label: 40/36/33/25/24/22%)
Evidence strength: moderate (mechanism generic)
Confidence: medium (anchored by quantitative human data for the same pathway; capped by direction assumption and generic mechanism)

AE: Hypertension
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA (via erythrocytosis → increased viscosity)
Relationship type: pathway_effect (secondary to erythrocytosis)
Supporting evidence: postmarketing disproportionality (3.4% vs 1.6%)
Evidence strength: weak-moderate
Confidence: low (extra inferential step, small/postmarketing-only frequency)

AE: Hypersensitivity reactions (including anaphylaxis/angioedema)
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA
Relationship type: pharmacological_support
Mechanistic chain: generic immunogenicity of a protein-based biologic directed at these ligands
Evidence strength: weak-moderate
Confidence: low (mechanism not protein-specific, frequency a reasoned estimate)

AE: Impaired fertility (male and female)
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA
Mechanistic chain: Activin A/B regulate pituitary FSH secretion and gonadal function (HPG axis); sustained neutralization disrupts folliculogenesis/spermatogenesis support
Evidence strength: moderate (established endocrine physiology + labeled warning for same pathway)
Confidence: low (no quantitative human frequency)

AE: Embryo-fetal toxicity
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA
Mechanistic chain: Activin/Nodal-family signaling is essential for early embryonic patterning and placental development; neutralization risks fetal harm
Evidence strength: moderate (labeled warning, established developmental physiology)
Confidence: low (no quantitative frequency; severe/fatal exception invoked)

AE: Cerebral haemorrhage
Protein(s): INHBB, INHBA (thrombocytopenia + vascular fragility convergence)
Evidence strength: weak (postmarketing signal only, confounded by comorbidities per source)
Confidence: low (kept only under severe/fatal exception)

AE: Worsening pulmonary vascular resistance / pulmonary arterial hypertension
Protein(s): GDF2, ENG, ACVRL1, BMPR2
Mechanistic chain: Human genetic loss-of-function in BMPR2/ACVRL1/ENG causes heritable PAH; pharmacologic neutralization of their ligand GDF2 could phenocopy reduced protective BMP9-ALK1-BMPR2 endothelial signaling over chronic exposure
Evidence strength: weak-moderate (strong genetic evidence for the pathway, but translation from partial pharmacological ligand reduction to clinical PAH is speculative)
Confidence: low (kept under severe/fatal exception)

**STEP 3: CROSS-PROTEIN CONVERGENCE**
- INHBB + INHBA jointly drive erythrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, bleeding events, reproductive/embryo-fetal effects (convergent_multi_protein_effect, same ligand family/receptor system).
- INHBB/INHBA (activin blockade) + GDF2/ENG/ACVRL1 (BMP9-ALK1 axis blockade) jointly converge on endothelial integrity, amplifying epistaxis/telangiectasia risk beyond what either pathway alone would produce (an HHT-like phenocopy).
- GDF2 + ENG + ACVRL1 + BMPR2 converge on the same pulmonary vascular homeostasis pathway, for which human genetics (heritable PAH) supports a shared severe risk.
- TGFBR1/TGFBR2 are flagged as uncertain/weak and do not independently support any AE given only animal evidence exists for TGFBR inhibitor toxicities (cartilage, valvulopathy) — these are excluded per the animal-evidence rule.

**STEP 4 / STEP 5**: All retained AEs trace to at least one likely/uncertain-perturbed protein, an explicit mechanism, and human-level evidence (pharmacological or genetic). Infections, cartilage/valvulopathy, and GPCR-mediated effects were excluded for lacking protein-level mechanism or adequate triage support.

**STEP 6: Overall severity distribution**
Weighting by estimated frequency: mild/moderate events (headache, epistaxis, rash, telangiectasia, diarrhea, dizziness, erythema, erythrocytosis, gingival bleeding, hypertension) dominate case volume; severe events (GI bleeding, thrombocytopenia, hypersensitivity, impaired fertility, embryo-fetal toxicity, PAH worsening) are less frequent; fatal (cerebral haemorrhage) is rare.
Approximate distribution: 90% mild/moderate, 9% severe, 1% fatal.

chunks.title: In vitro characterization of prostanoid receptors on human myometrium at term pregnancy.
chunks.text: 1. Prostanoid receptors present on the pregnant human myometrium in vitro have been characterized according to the receptor classification proposed by Coleman et al. (1984) using natural prostanoids and synthetic, selective analogues and antagonists where available. 2. Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) produced a biphasic effect consisting of an initial excitation followed by a dose-related inhibition. The EP2/EP3-receptor agonists, rioprostil and misoprostol, produced similar effects to PGE2, however, the excitatory event of the misoprostol response was related to dose. The EP1/EP3-receptor agonist, sulprostone, evoked a purely excitatory response which was unaffected by AH6809. The selective EP2-receptor agonist butaprost produced a long-lasting dose-dependent inhibition of activity. The results from these prostanoids indicated that inhibitory EP2- and excitatory EP3-receptors are present on myometrium from pregnant donors at term. 3. PGF2 alpha and the synthetic FP-receptor agonist, fluprostenol, caused equipotent excitatory effects, indicating the presence of contractile FP-receptors. 4. PGD2 produced a biphasic effect of which the inhibition appeared dose-related and was antagonized by the selective DP-receptor antagonist BW A868C. The selective DP-receptor agonist, BW245C, produced a potent inhibitory effect that was competitively antagonized by BW A868C (pA2 = 8.6). 5. PGI2 produced a biphasic response qualitatively similar to PGE2. The EP1/IP-receptor agonist, iloprost, produced an occasional unquantifiable excitation and dose-related inhibition. The selective IP-receptor prostanoid, cicaprost, evoked only an inhibitory response. 6. The stable thromboxane A2 (TXA2)-mimetic, U46619, produced potent excitation which was competitively antagonized by the TP-receptor antagonist, GR32191 (pA2 = 7.2). 7. The prostanoids tested indicate that a heterogeneous population of prostanoid receptors are presen ton human myometrium from pregnant donors. It may be concluded that excitation is EP3-, FP- and TP-receptor-mediated and inhibition is EP2-, DP- and IP-receptor-mediated. Comparison of data obtained from non-pregnant specimens indicates that the lower segment tissue from pregnant donors demonstrated more pronounced responses to EP2 and IP-receptor activation.

chunks.title: Interaction of prostanoid EP₃ and TP receptors in guinea-pig isolated aorta: contractile self-synergism of 11-deoxy-16,16-dimethyl PGE₂.
chunks.text:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Surprisingly high contractile activity was reported for 11-deoxy-16,16-dimethyl prostaglandin E₂ (DX-DM PGE₂) on pig cerebral artery when used as a selective EP₃ receptor agonist. This study investigated the selectivity profile of DX-DM PGE₂, focusing on the interaction between its EP₃ and TP (thromboxane A₂-like) agonist activities.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Contraction of guinea-pig trachea (EP₁ system) and aorta (EP₃ and TP systems) was measured in conventional organ baths.
KEY RESULTS: Strong contraction of guinea-pig aorta to sulprostone and 17-phenyl PGE₂ (EP₃ agonists) was only seen under priming with a second contractile agent such as phenylephrine, histamine or U-46619 (TP agonist). In contrast, DX-DM PGE₂ induced strong contraction, which on the basis of treatment with (DG)-3ap (EP₃ antagonist) and/or BMS-180291 (TP antagonist) was attributed to self-synergism arising from co-activation of EP₃ and TP receptors. EP₃/TP self-synergism also accounted for contraction induced by PGF(2α) and its analogues (+)-cloprostenol and latanoprost-FA. DX-DM PGE₂ also showed significant EP₁ agonism on guinea-pig trachea as defined by the EP₁ antagonists SC-51322, (ONO)-5-methyl-1 and AH-6809, although AH-6809 exhibited poor specificity at concentrations ≥3 µM.
CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: EP₃/TP self-synergism, as seen with PGE/PGF analogues in this study, may confound EP₃ agonist potency comparisons and the characterization of prostanoid receptor systems. The competitive profile of a TP antagonist may be distorted by variation in the silent/overt contraction profile of the EP₃ system in different studies. The relevance of self-synergism to in vivo actions of natural prostanoid receptor agonists is discussed.

chunks.title: Postmarketing analysis of sotatercept: identifying serious unlabelled events.
mesh_terms: United States Food and Drug Administration
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
chunks.text: Cerebral haemorrhage may be linked to sotatercept’s haematological effects, including thrombocytopenia, which could exacerbate bleeding risk, particularly in patients receiving concomitant anticoagulants or antiplatelet therapies. Additionally, sotatercept-associated hypertension (3.4% vs 1.6% in the pooled PULSAR/STELLAR analysis) might contribute to cerebral vascular stress, while its mechanism as an activin signalling inhibitor may theoretically influence vascular remodelling and microvascular integrity, as suggested by telangiectasia development. However, establishing definitive causality is challenging given the multifactorial nature of cerebral haemorrhage in patients with PAH, where disease progression, concurrent medications (particularly anticoagulants), comorbidities and baseline bleeding risks may all contribute to these events. Nevertheless, identifying these potential safety signals through early postmarketing surveillance provides valuable clinical warnings that warrant further investigation. Controlled studies with adequate confounder adjustment are needed to clarify the true relationship between sotatercept and cerebral haemorrhage. Ascites may reflect the progression of right heart dysfunction in advanced PAH. Although sotatercept improves pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular remodelling, transient haemodynamic shifts or the unmasking of latent left ventricular dysfunction (due to reduced right heart afterload) could paradoxically exacerbate systemic congestion in vulnerable individuals. In addition, patients with PAH and comorbid portal hypertension (eg, from heritable or connective tissue disease-associated subtypes) may be more susceptible to ascites due to splanchnic venous congestion, though this remains speculative. Clarification of whether these events are linked to disease progression or sotatercept’s pharmacodynamics is needed, but current data are insufficient for definitive conclusions. Prospective studies are required to clarify these relationships. Until then, clinicians should remain vigilant for ascites in sotatercept-treated patients. Gender-specific and reporter-specific analyses reveal distinct patterns in the safety profile of sotatercept. Women contributed a greater number of AE reports, which aligns with the higher prevalence of PAH in the female population. However, the disproportionality signal for haematological abnormalities was stronger among men, suggesting that haemoglobin and haematocrit elevations, though less frequent, tend to be more pronounced in male patients. The underlying cause remains uncertain, but it may reflect sex-related differences in drug-induced erythropoiesis or baseline haematological parameters that accentuate these changes in men, warranting further investigation to elucidate these mechanisms. chunks.title: Nonclinical Profile of PF-06952229 (MDV6058), a Novel TGFβRI/Activin Like Kinase 5 Inhibitor Supports Clinical Evaluation in Cancer.
chunks.journal: The Journal of pharmacology and experimental therapeutics
mesh_terms: Receptor, Transforming Growth Factor-beta Type I
chunks.text: The development of transforming growth factor βreceptor inhibitors (TGFβRi) as new medicines has been affected by cardiac valvulopathy and arteriopathy toxicity findings in nonclinical toxicology studies. PF-06952229 (MDV6058) selected using rational drug design is a potent and selective TGFβRI inhibitor with a relatively clean off-target selectivity profile and good pharmacokinetic properties across species. PF-06952229 inhibited clinically translatable phospho-SMAD2 biomarker (≥60%) in human and cynomolgus monkey peripheral blood mononuclear cells, as well as in mouse and rat splenocytes. Using an optimized, intermittent dosing schedule (7-day on/7-day off/cycle; 5 cycles), PF-06952229 demonstrated efficacy in a 63-day syngeneic MC38 colon carcinoma mouse model. In the pivotal repeat-dose toxicity studies (rat and cynomolgus monkey), PF-06952229 on an intermittent dosing schedule (5-day on/5-day off cycle; 5 cycles, 28 doses) showed no cardiac-related adverse findings. However, new toxicity findings related to PF-06952229 included reversible hepatocellular (hepatocyte necrosis with corresponding clinically monitorable transaminase increases) and lung (hemorrhage with mixed cell inflammation) findings at ≥ targeted projected clinical efficacious exposures. Furthermore, partially reversible cartilage hypertrophy (trachea and femur in rat; femur in monkey) and partially to fully reversible, clinically monitorable decreases in serum phosphorus and urinary phosphate at ≥ projected clinically efficacious exposures were observed. Given the integral role of TGFβ in endochondral bone formation, cartilage findings in toxicity studies have been observed with other TGFβRi classes of compounds. The favorable cumulative profile of PF-06952229 in biochemical, pharmacodynamic, pharmacokinetic, and nonclinical studies allowed for its evaluation in cancer patients using the intermittent dosing schedule (7-day on/7-day off) and careful protocol-defined monitoring. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Only a few TGFβRi have progressed for clinical evaluation due to adverse cardiac findings in pivotal nonclinical toxicity studies. The potential translations of such findings in patients are of major concern. Using a carefully optimized intermittent dosing schedule, PF-06952229 has demonstrated impressive pharmacological efficacy in the syngeneic MC38 colon carcinoma mouse model. Additionally, a nonclinical toxicology package without cardiovascular liabilities and generally monitorable toxicity profile has been completed. The compound presents an acceptable International Conference on Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Registration of Pharmaceuticals for Human Use S9-compliant profile for the intended-to-treat cancer patients.

chunks.title: Drug-induced Physeal Abnormalities in Preclinical Toxicity Studies.
mesh_terms: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
chunks.text: Most toxic physeal changes are characterized microscopically by altered chondrocyte development, proliferation, or maturation in the growth plate and eventually result in disordered appositional bone growth. Many therapeutic drugs directly or indirectly target proteins involved in chondrocytic differentiation and maturation pathways, so toxic physeal injury has become increasingly common in preclinical toxicologic pathology. While physeal dysplasia has been associated with several different drug classes including bisphosphonates, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor inhibitors, fibroblast growth factor receptor inhibitors, transforming growth factor beta receptor inhibitors, and vascular targeting agents, physeal changes often share similar morphologic features including thickening and disorganization of the hypertrophic layer, increased numbers of hypertrophic chondrocytes, altered mineralization of endochondral ossification, and/or increased thickness of subphyseal bone. Knowledge of genetic and nutritional diseases affecting bone growth has been important in helping to determine which specific target drugs may be affecting that could result in toxic physeal lesions. A pathophysiologic mechanism for most physeal toxicants has been determined in detail using a variety of investigative techniques. However, due to the signaling cross talk and the tight regulation required for chondrocyte maturation in the physis, several growth factor pathways are likely to be affected simultaneously with pharmacologic disruption of physeal homeostasis and inhibition of one factor necessary for chondrocyte function often affects others.

chunks.title: Postmarketing analysis of sotatercept: identifying serious unlabelled events.
mesh_terms: United States Food and Drug Administration
Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
chunks.text: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Sotatercept, a first-in-class activin signalling inhibitor, represents a novel therapeutic advancement for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a progressive and life-threatening condition characterised by pulmonary vascular remodelling and right ventricular dysfunction. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS The first large-scale Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System analysis, 48 safety signals (18 unlabelled) and the critical discovery of cerebral haemorrhage and ascites as important medical events. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Emphasises the clinical implications for monitoring protocols and regulatory pharmacovigilance. Introduction Sotatercept, a first-in-class activin signalling inhibitor, represents a novel therapeutic advancement for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a progressive and life-threatening condition characterised by pulmonary vascular remodelling and right ventricular dysfunction. By targeting the imbalance between proproliferative activin signalling and antiproliferative bone morphogenetic protein pathways, sotatercept addresses the underlying pathophysiology of PAH, offering potential disease-modifying effects. Clinical trials, including the pivotal PULSAR and STELLAR studies, have demonstrated its efficacy in reducing pulmonary vascular resistance, improving exercise capacity and delaying clinical worsening. These findings supported its Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval on 26 March 2024 for adults with PAH, establishing it as a critical addition to existing therapies. Despite its therapeutic benefits, emerging safety data from clinical trials highlight specific risks, including thrombocytopenia, haemoglobin elevation and telangiectasia. Notably, the ZENITH trial identified life-threatening adverse events (AEs)—including cardiac arrest—in patients with advanced PAH, highlighting potential risks in vulnerable populations. Following sotatercept’s FDA approval and the limitations of premarketing studies, including small sample sizes and controlled environments, postmarketing pharmacovigilance is vital to evaluate its safety in diverse real-world populations. This pharmacovigilance study uses real-world data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) to systematically evaluate the safety profile of sotatercept. We identified key safety signals by quantifying AE frequency and disproportionality, investigated unlisted preferred terms (PTs) to detect potential risks and classified AEs by severity using the EudraVigilance Expert Working Group’s IME (Important Medical Events) list (V.28.0). By integrating these analyses, this study aims to bridge knowledge gaps between clinical trial evidence and real-world safety outcomes, ensuring safer utilisation of this groundbreaking

chunks.title: The short-term effects of repetitive E. coli-derived rhBMP-2 administration through intravenous injection in rats.
chunks.text: Escherichia coli-derived recombinant human (rh)BMP-2 (E.BMP-2) can be used as a bone graft substitute because to its high osteoinductivity, but its toxicity is not well understood. Thus, we report on the toxicity of E.BMP-2 in Sprague-Dawley rats under the condition of repetitive injection for 2 weeks. Randomly selected 10 male and female rats were administered with E.BMP-2 at a dose of 0.05, 0.18 or 0.5 mg/kg as an experimental group. A control group with another 10 rats was given E.BMP-2 carrier. Both E.BMP-2 and E.BMP-2 carrier were administered through intravenous injection for 2 weeks. For toxicokinetics study, 3 male and female rats were randomly selected from each group. During the observation period, general symptom, weight and food intakes were monitored, and ophthalmic and urine tests were performed as well. After the observation period, all animals were subjected to blood test, biochemical analysis and organ-weight measurement. During autopsy, visual inspections and histopathological examinations were done. Toxicokinetics study confirmed systemic exposure of the test material. No death or abnormal clinical sign was found during the injection period. Toxicity changes induced by the injection were not detected in autopsy or the tests for weight, food intakes, ophthalmology, hematology and serum biochemistry. The female groups administered with 0.18 and 0.5 mg/kg (the female 0.18-mg/kg group and the female 0.5-mg/kg group) showed absolute and relative weight loss in ovaries and reduced corpora lutea. It was the expected pharmacologic activity, rather than toxicity. The histopathological test revealed cartilage formation and increased fibroblast around the tail vein, but these were thought to be the result of osteoinductivity of the test material. In the male group with 0.5 mg/kg of E.BMP-2 (the male 0.5-mg/kg group), local appearance of multinucleated cells in lung parenchyma was observed, but it was considered as the natural reaction to remove E.BMP-2, which is a recombinant protein. In toxicokinetics study, systemic exposure (area under the serum concentration-time curve and maximum observed serum concentration) increased as the injection dose was increased in both male and female rats, and no clear difference was noticed between the sexes. Blood drug content did not change during the injection period, but the half-life was shortened as the injection dose was increased. Under the condition of this study, the no observed adverse effects level of E.BMP-2 was over 0.5 mg/kg in both male and female rats.

chunks.title: FDA label: BIMATOPROST (Bimatoprost)
chunks.text:
Adverse reactions: 6 ADVERSE REACTIONS The following adverse reactions are described elsewhere in the labeling: • Pigmentation [see Warnings and Precautions (5.1) ] • Eyelash Changes [see Warnings and Precautions (5.2) ] • Intraocular Inflammation [see Warnings and Precautions (5.3) ] • Macular Edema [see Warnings and Precautions (5.4) ] • Hypersensitivity [see Contraindications (4) ] Most common adverse reaction (45%) is conjunctival hyperemia ( 6.1 ). To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact Aurobindo Pharma USA, Inc. at 1-866-850-2876 or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch . 6.1 Clinical Trials Experience Because clinical trials are conducted under widely varying conditions, adverse reaction rates observed in the clinical trials of a drug cannot be directly compared to rates in the clinical trials of another drug and may not reflect the rates observed in practice. In clinical trials, the most frequent events associated with the use of bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03% occurring in approximately 15% to 45% of patients, in descending order of incidence, included conjunctival hyperemia, growth of eyelashes, and ocular pruritus. Approximately 3% of patients discontinued therapy due to conjunctival hyperemia. Ocular adverse events occurring in approximately 3 to 10% of patients, in descending order of incidence, included ocular dryness, visual disturbance, ocular burning, foreign body sensation, eye pain, pigmentation of the periocular skin, blepharitis, cataract, superficial punctate keratitis, periorbital erythema, ocular irritation, and eyelash darkening. The following ocular adverse events reported in approximately 1 to 3% of patients, in descending order of incidence, included: eye discharge, tearing, photophobia, allergic conjunctivitis, asthenopia, increases in iris pigmentation, and conjunctival edema. In less than 1% of patients, intraocular inflammation was reported as iritis. Systemic adverse events reported in approximately 10% of patients were infections (primarily colds and upper respiratory tract infections). The following systemic adverse events reported in approximately 1 to 5% of patients, in descending order of incidence, included headaches, abnormal liver function tests, asthenia and hirsutism. 6.2 Postmarketing Experience The following adverse reactions have been identified during postapproval use of bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03%. Because these reactions are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size, it is not always possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to drug exposure. The reactions, which have been chosen for inclusion due to either their seriousness, frequency of reporting, possible causal connection to bimatoprost ophthalmic solution, or a combination of these factors, include: abnormal hair growth, asthma-like symptoms, dizziness, dyspnea, eyelid edema, hypersensitivity reaction including signs and symptoms of eye allergy and allergic dermatitis, hypertension, nausea, and periorbital and lid changes associated with periorbital fat atrophy leading to skin tightness, deepening of the eyelid sulcus, eyelid ptosis, enophthalmos and eyelid retraction; and skin discoloration (non-periocular).

Warnings and precautions (excerpt): 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS Pigmentation : Pigmentation of the iris, periorbital tissue (eyelid) and eyelashes can occur. Iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent. ( 5.1 ) Eyelash Changes : Gradual change to eyelashes including increased length, thickness and number of lashes. Usually reversible. ( 5.2 ) 5.1 Pigmentation Bimatoprost ophthalmic solution has been reported to cause changes to pigmented tissues. The most frequently reported changes have been increased pigmentation of the iris, periorbital tissue (eyelid) and eyelashes. Pigmentation is expected to increase as long as bimatoprost is administered. The pigmentation change is due to increased melanin content in the melanocytes rather than to an increase in the number of melanocytes. After discontinuation of bimatoprost, pigmentation of the iris is likely to be permanent, while pigmentation of the periorbital tissue and eyelash changes have been reported to be reversible in some patients. Patients who receive treatment should be informed of the possibility of increased pigmentation. The long term effects of increased pigmentation are not known. Iris color change may not be noticeable for several months to years. Typically, the brown pigmentation around the pupil spreads concentrically towards the periphery of the iris and the entire iris or parts of the iris become more brownish. Neither nevi nor freckles of the iris appear to be affected by treatment. While treatment with bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03% can [...]

chunks.title: FDA label: CARBOPROST (CARBOPROST TROMETHAMINE)
chunks.text: Adverse reactions: ADVERSE REACTIONS The adverse effects of carboprost tromethamine sterile solution are generally transient and reversible when therapy ends. The most frequent adverse reactions observed are related to its contractile effect on smooth muscle. In patients studied, approximately two-thirds experienced vomiting and diarrhea, approximately one-third had nausea, one-eighth had a temperature increase greater than 2° F, and one-fourteenth experienced flushing. The pretreatment or concurrent administration of antiemetic and antidiarrheal drugs decreases considerably the very high incidence of gastrointestinal effects common with all prostaglandins used for abortion. Their use should be considered an integral part of the management of patients undergoing abortion with carboprost tromethamine. Of those patients experiencing a temperature elevation, approximately one-sixteenth had a clinical diagnosis of endometritis. The remaining temperature elevations returned to normal within several hours after the last injection. Adverse effects observed during the use of carboprost tromethamine injection for abortion and for hemorrhage, not all of which are clearly drug related, in decreasing order of frequency include: Vomiting Nervousness Diarrhea Nosebleed Nausea Sleep disorders Flushing or hot flashes Dyspnea Chills or shivering Tightness in chest Coughing Wheezing Headaches Posterior cervical Endometritis perforation Weakness Hiccough Diaphoresis Dysmenorrhea-like pain Dizziness Paresthesia Blurred vision Backache Epigastric pain Muscular pain Excessive thirst Breast tenderness Twitching eyelids Eye pain Gagging, retching Drowsiness Dry throat Dystonia Sensation of choking Asthma Thyroid storm Injection site pain Syncope Tinnitus Palpitations Vertigo Rash Vaso-vagal syndrome Upper respiratory infection Dryness of mouth Hyperventilation Leg cramps Respiratory distress Perforate uterus Perforated uterus Hematemesis Anxiety Taste alterations Chest pain Urinary tract infection Retained placental fragment Septic shock Torticollis Shortness of breath Lethargy Fullness of throat Hypertension Uterine sacculation Tachycardia Faintness, light-headedness Pulmonary edema Endometritis from IUCD Uterine rupture The most common complications when carboprost tromethamine injection was utilized for abortion requiring additional treatment after discharge from the hospital were endometritis, retained placental fragments, and excessive uterine bleeding, occurring in about one in every 50 patients. Post-marketing experience: Hypersensitivity reactions (e.g. Anaphylactic reaction, Anaphylactic shock, Anaphylactoid reaction, Angioedema).

chunks.title: FDA label: ALPROSTADIL (Alprostadil)
chunks.text:
Boxed warning: WARNING Apnea is experienced by about 10 to 12% of neonates with congenital heart defects treated with alprostadil injection. Apnea is most often seen in neonates weighing less than 2 kg at birth and usually appears during the first hour of drug infusion. Therefore, respiratory status should be monitored throughout treatment, and alprostadil injection should be used where ventilatory assistance is immediately available.

Adverse reactions: ADVERSE REACTIONS Central Nervous System Apnea has been reported in about 12% of the neonates treated (see WARNING box). Other common adverse reactions reported have been fever in about 14% of the patients treated and seizures in about 4%. The following reactions have been reported in less than 1% of the patients: cerebral bleeding, hyperextension of the neck, hyperirritability, hypothermia, jitteriness, lethargy, and stiffness. Cardiovascular System The most common adverse reactions reported have been flushing in about 10% of patients (more common after intraarterial dosing), bradycardia in about 7%, hypotension in about 4%, tachycardia in about 3%, cardiac arrest in about 1%, and edema in about 1%. The following reactions have been reported in less than 1% of the patients: congestive heart failure, hyperemia, second degree heart block, shock, spasm of the right ventricle infundibulum, supraventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation. Respiratory System The following reactions have been reported in less than 1% of the patients: bradypnea, bronchial wheezing, hypercapnia, respiratory depression, respiratory distress, and tachypnea. Gastrointestinal System See WARNINGS . The most common adverse reaction reported has been diarrhea in about 2% of the patients. The following reactions have been reported in less than 1% of the patients: gastric regurgitation, and hyperbilirubinemia. Hematologic System The most common hematologic event reported has been disseminated intravascular coagulation in about 1% of the patients. The following events have been reported in less than 1% of the patients: anemia, bleeding, and thrombocytopenia. Excretory System Anuria and hematuria have been reported in less than 1% of the patients. Skeletal System Cortical proliferation of the long bones has been reported (see PRECAUTIONS ). Miscellaneous Sepsis has been reported in about 2% of the patients. Peritonitis has been reported in less than 1% of the patients. Hypokalemia has been reported in about 1%, and hypoglycemia and hyperkalemia have been reported in less than 1% of the patients. To report SUSPECTED ADVERSE REACTIONS, contact Meitheal Pharmaceuticals, Inc. at 1-844-824-8426 or FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or www.fda.gov/medwatch .

Warnings: WARNINGS See WARNING box. NOTE : Alprostadil injection must be diluted before it is administered. See dilution instructions in DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION section. The administration of alprostadil injection to neonates may result in gastric outlet obstruction secondary to antral hyperplasia. This effect appears to be related to duration of therapy and cumulative dose of the drug. Neonates receiving alprostadil injection at recommended doses for more than 120 hours should be closely monitored for evidence of antral hyperplasia and gastric outlet obstruction. Alprostadil injection should be infused for the shortest time and at the lowest dose that will produce the desired effects. The risks of long-term infusion of alprostadil injection should be weighed against the possible benefits that critically ill infants may derive from its administration.

chunks.title: Toxic role of prostaglandin E2 receptor EP1 after intracerebral hemorrhage in mice.
